name: Umar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Umar. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a jumbo at Kingsgate, an underground gold mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two big arms, and I drill the face, about sixty holes in a pattern, so the charge-up crew can load them with explosives and blast the next few metres of tunnel. Shift starts at six, I check the ground, scale down any loose rock, set up and drill. When the round pulls clean, meaning the blast breaks the whole face, that's a good day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The heat at the bottom of the decline, and the water, everything's wet. And waiting, when the ventilation's down or the loader's broken and you just sit. I fill the waiting with my phone, mostly managing the rental unit I bought last year. Sara (my fiancée) says I'm the only person who does property admin three hundred metres underground.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use one to keep track of the rental, write to the tenants, check my budget, and I used it to compare mortgage offers. At work I've been asking it about the drill pattern software, because Kingsgate is trialling tele-remote drilling from the surface. My dad thinks I'm mad, he says a man should learn one trade well. I think you learn one trade well and keep your eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. The tools are still useful, and I keep my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overdone but the tools are real. At crib I'd show the boys how I use it for the rental, because a few of them want to buy property. Online I'd post a bit about what works and what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me this is a good world. Gold is high, Kingsgate has fifteen years of ore, and I'm on top pay for my age. Nothing big changes, so I keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling, and I'd buy a second rental unit next year with the savings. I'd keep at the tele-remote trial, because even a slow change is a better seat. And Sara and I would get married in the spring as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Gold could drop, but there are two other underground mines within an hour, and I could get on at either. I've got about a year of costs saved besides the property.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second rental at twenty-seven. Some would call that risky. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the opposite of reckless. A rental is something real, bricks and rent. My dad's generation trusted the company and the pension. I'd rather own something.

say: The hype was **overdone**, but the tools are real.
He'd show the crew how he uses AI to **manage a rental**.
think: **Gold is high** and Kingsgate has fifteen years of ore.
Nothing big changes, so he **keeps building** his assets.
do: Buy a **second rental unit** next year with savings.
Marry Sara in the **spring** as planned.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased with how things look.
S0.quote: My dad's generation trusted the company and the pension. I'd rather own something.
fieldNote: He sees property as **independence** from the employer.
He uses AI daily but keeps a **traditional** view of family and ownership.
With **nearby mines** and savings, he is truly secure here.

steps.text: Keep drilling the face at Kingsgate on the jumbo
Buy a second rental unit in town next year
Marry Sara in the spring as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. It's already starting at Kingsgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, not a threat, if you move early. I'd tell the boys to put their names down for the tele-remote course now. Online I'd say the same, learn it or watch someone else learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the jumbo goes tele-remote within three or four years, run from a room on the surface. That's fine for me. I'd rather drill from a chair in air-conditioning than in thirty-five degrees and water up to my ankles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote course in the first six months and push to be one of the first on the surface. I'd keep using AI to learn the drill design side, so I could move toward drill and blast planning. And I'd keep buying property, slowly, one unit every couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A bit sorry for the older blokes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle with this at Kingsgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them will hate it. Kev (the shift boss) is sixty and has never used a computer. I'd offer to show him, but some men would rather retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the company owes them anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's their choice. I don't think the company owes anyone a job for life. But a good company trains its people, and Kingsgate has, so far.

say: It's **a chance**, not a threat, if you move early.
He'd tell the crew to **put their names down** for tele-remote now.
think: The jumbo goes **tele-remote** within three or four years.
He'd rather drill from a **surface chair** than in heat and water.
do: Take the **tele-remote course** in the first six months.
Use AI to learn **drill and blast** planning.
Keep buying property, about **one unit** every two years.
feel: Mostly **good**, a bit sorry for older workers.
S1.quote: I'd rather drill from a chair in air-conditioning than in thirty-five degrees and water up to my ankles.
fieldNote: He welcomes the change as a **better seat**, not a loss.
His free-market view shows: **no job for life**, but good firms train people.
He offers to help **Kev (the shift boss)**, but accepts some will retire.

steps.text: Take the tele-remote drilling course within six months
Use AI to study drill and blast planning
Buy another rental unit about every two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not a better seat anymore. That's no seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: the people who own things will be fine and the people who only have a wage won't. I'd tell everyone at work to own something, a house, a unit, shares in the mine. I'd say the government shouldn't stop it, but it shouldn't pretend it's painless either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the tele-remote job is gone. If AI can plan and drill the face by 2028 from a screen, and robots can do the scaling and charging by 2031, there's nothing underground for me. My plan was ten years of good pay and property. I'd get maybe four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze the first two years hard. Every overtime shift, and I'd put it into paying down the rental mortgage so it's clear by 2031. I'd look at buying a small earthmoving machine, a mini excavator, and running it with AI scheduling for house sites, because hands-on work on small jobs lasts longer than in the mines. And Sara and I would still marry, but we'd rent instead of buying our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, I've got the unit and savings. But I didn't think it would be this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Sara everything, or protect her from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd tell Sara the truth. She works as a pharmacy assistant, and her job's in trouble too with the thinking AI first. We'd plan together, and lean on our families if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the earthmoving plan risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Everyone's going to want the same small jobs once the mines go. But I'd rather be early with a machine than late with nothing.

Government shouldn't stop it, but **shouldn't pretend** it's painless.
think: The **tele-remote job** disappears once AI can plan and drill.
His ten-year plan shrinks to **about four years** of good pay.
do: Pay down the **rental mortgage** to clear it by 2031.
Buy a **mini excavator** and book house-site work with AI scheduling.
Rent after the wedding instead of **buying a home**.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, surprised by the speed.
S2.quote: The people who own things will be fine and the people who only have a wage won't.
fieldNote: His **property strategy** becomes his main defence.
Sara's **pharmacy job** is hit first, so both incomes are at risk.
He uses the **robot gap** to start a small hands-on business.

steps.text: Pay off the rental unit's mortgage by 2031
Buy a mini excavator and take small house-site jobs
Use AI scheduling to book and price excavator jobs
Rent a home after the wedding instead of buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get set up, if you start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. I'd tell the younger miners to buy something and learn a second thing. I'd be pretty loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get three years on tele-remote, then a few more on surface work, and the underground jobs go around 2034. That's long enough to have two rentals mostly paid off and a small business running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote course and take that job. I'd buy the second unit next year as planned. Around 2029 I'd buy the mini excavator and start weekend jobs, so the business is already going when mining dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see my way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay loyal to Kingsgate to the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Kingsgate's been good to me, but I'm not going to wait to find out how good. Leaving on my own terms is better than being let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sara start a family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, around thirty. Sara wants children soon after the wedding and so do I. Five years is long enough to do that properly.

Young miners should **buy something** and learn a second skill.
think: Underground jobs go around **2034**, after a few years on tele-remote.
That's long enough for **two rentals** and a small business.
do: Take the **tele-remote** job after the course.
Buy the **second unit** next year as planned.
feel: **Uneasy**, but he can see a way through.
S3.quote: Leaving on my own terms is better than being let go.
fieldNote: He plans to **leave before** being pushed, unlike older peers.
The **side business** starts early so it's running when mining ends.
Family plans go ahead because five years gives **enough time**.

steps.text: Take the tele-remote drilling job at Kingsgate
Buy the second rental unit next year
Start weekend mini excavator jobs around 2029
Start a family with Sara around age thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a full plan, start to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's fine if people get moving. Ten years is a whole apprenticeship and a business. I'd still tell everyone to own something, a unit, a machine or shares, before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. I'd do tele-remote, then drill and blast planning, then step out around thirty-five into the earthmoving business or property full-time. By the time robots come for hands-on work, I'm the one owning the robots, not driving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling, do the courses, buy a unit every two or three years, and start the excavator business around year five. Use AI for the books and the quotes. Get married, have kids, and send them to school knowing all this is normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a good long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting too comfortable. If it's ten years away, people stop paying attention. I'd check my plan every year with Sara, on our anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara has to agree to every bit of it. We decide money things together. That's how my parents ran their house, and it worked.

He'd keep telling everyone to **own something**: a unit, a machine or shares.

When robots arrive, he wants to be **owning them**, not driving them.

Start the **excavator business** around year five, with AI doing the books.
feel: **Calm**, like looking down a good long road.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even with property and savings, two years isn't long enough to build anything that replaces a mining wage. What would help is cheap loans for workers to buy machines or start a small business, not handouts, and the mine giving us real notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether ordinary workers can own a piece of the robots. If the mine's machines do the work, the people of the town should be able to buy shares in them. That's the free market working for us, not just for the owners.

headlineQuote: If the mine's machines do the work, the people of the town should be able to buy shares in them.
portrait: Umar, 27, operates a **jumbo drill** underground at Kingsgate, a gold mine.
He is engaged to **Sara**, a pharmacy assistant, and already owns one rental unit.
He uses **AI daily** but holds traditional views on family and self-reliance.
Slow change looks like a **better seat** to him; AGI by 2028 cuts his plan to four years.
His answer to every picture is to **own something**: property, a machine, shares.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years can't build a replacement for a mining wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for workers to buy machines or start businesses.
Real **notice** from the mine before automation.
